For LINE with negative sampling and edge sampling, the overall training time complexity is typically expressed as O(NE × NS × d), where NE is the number of edges, NS is the number of negative samples per positive edge, and d is the embedding dimension. If edge sampling is used to subsample training edges, the effective cost becomes proportional to the number of sampled edges rather than all possible vertex pairs, so the runtime is linear in the observed edge set and the sampling budget.

The reason this complexity is independent of the number of vertices |V| is that LINE does not enumerate all vertices during training. Instead, each update only touches the two endpoints of a sampled edge plus a small, fixed number of negative samples. Because the per-update work depends on the embedding dimension and the sampling parameters, not on scanning the full vertex set, increasing |V| alone does not increase the asymptotic training cost unless it also changes the number of sampled edges or negative samples.

In short: the model’s training cost scales with edges and samples, not with the total vertex count, because optimization is performed on sampled local interactions rather than on all vertices globally.
